sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Purpose of the gross-to-net walk
sections.what: Explains that the bridge takes a gross benefit and subtracts three named costs to reach a net benefit. The file lists the four steps and states that cost ends are matched in the cautious direction.
sections.why: Stated in the docstring: every subtraction is named so a reader can see it, rather than a fluent narrative hiding a mismatch.
sections.watch_out: A low case that pairs optimistic benefit with optimistic cost hides the downside, so the cost band must stay opposite to the benefit band.

sections.name: walk
sections.title: Building one currency's bridge
sections.what: Builds the bridge for one currency. It subtracts the three costs from the gross benefit, crossing the ends so the low net uses high costs, and records whether run cost was priced.
sections.why: Stated in the docstring: the run-cost flag travels with the number, so a reader cannot see a net that silently excludes run cost.
sections.watch_out: If the run-cost flag is set wrongly, the net will look higher than it should, and nothing else in the output will warn about it.

summary: Builds the gross-to-net benefit bridge for one currency, showing each cost as a named line with its own range.
purpose: Shows how a gross benefit becomes a net benefit after prerequisite, implementation and run costs, so reviewers can trace the figure.
why: Stated in the docstring: an earlier prose bridge looked right but did not add up. Crossing the cost ends keeps the low case a real downside.
how: Sort the process IDs. Work out the net range by subtracting the high cost ends from the low benefit, the base costs from the base benefit, and the low cost ends from the high benefit. Round each line for display, then return one bridge object.
inputs: A currency code, the process IDs, the gross benefit range, three cost ranges, and a flag saying whether run cost was priced.
outputs: A bridge object holding each line and the net range, rounded for display.
risks: The crossed ends are easy to break in a later edit. The run-cost flag is passed in by the caller and is not checked here. A caller who forgets the flag gets a net that looks higher with no warning.
debug: If net looks too high, check that run cost was actually calculated and the flag is set honestly. If the low net is above the base net, the ends were probably swapped. Compare each line against the net to check it adds up.
